newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Arab Americans try to shake off "terrorist" image.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Arab Americans try to shake off "terrorist" image.

text.p: Two mothers were walking to a Seven-Eleven store in Virginia to buy candy for their kids recently when they were arrested.
Their crime? Wearing a veil.
The women were Arab Americans, an increasingly prosperous but little-understood piece of the American ethnic mosaic.
"There's a great misunderstanding of our culture and of Islam in America," said Hala Maksoud, president of the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee (ADC).
"There's a law against wearing masks in Virginia, something to do with combating the Ku Klux Klan," she said with irony. "The police later apologised profusely."
Maksoud is full of stories of ignorance or discrimination towards the United States' estimated three million Arabs, most of whom are Christian.
Arabs are "demonised" in the media as terrorists and portrayed in movies and cartoons as villains, she says.
"After TWA Flight 800, people were again really frightened that fingers would be pointed at us," she said, referring to the airliner crash off Long Island, New York, last July.
The cause of the crash is still unknown but a bomb was at first suspected.
"The only violent act by Arabs was the World Trade Centre bombing," said James Zogby, head of the Arab American Institute.
The bombers were a fringe group from Egypt with no support among Arab Americans, Zogby contends.
Zogby believes Arabs will get the respect they deserve only if they are strong politically. He is leading a drive to register Arab voters and has forged close ties with the Clinton White House.
"We don't want America to be a place for people to settle their scores. The World Trade Centre was a huge blow for us," Zogby said.
Two-thirds of Arab Americans were born in the United States and consider themselves Americans, he says.
More than half are Christian, of Lebanese, Syrian, Palestinian and Egyptian Copt origin. Typically, they own their own businesses and are well-educated.
More recent waves of immigrants are Moslems such as Shi'ite Lebanese who have settled in Dearborn, Michigan, or Palestinians in Chicago, studies show.
A poll of Arab Americans by Zogby's Institute in October showed that most Arabs maintained close ties with the Middle East and supported a Palestinian state alongside Israel.
But on a list of seven issues in the current U.S. presidential campaign they ranked foreign policy last, behind concerns such as education, crime, drugs and health care.
Even if they want to, Arab Americans cannot forget the Middle East and particularly the Palestinian-Israeli conflict, Maksoud believes.
"We can't shield ourselves from what happens over there. The problems we have here are because of the problems we have there," she says.

"The United States has discovered Arab Americans only as a result of conflict, in '67 and '73, the oil embargo, Iran, Lebanon...This has been exploited by organisations which have a stake in dehumanising Arabs or Moslems, I mean Zionist organisations," Maksoud added.

Zogby credits Benjamin Netanyahu, before he became Israeli prime minister, with helping mould the image of the Arab as terrorist among right-wing and neo-conservative American opinion-makers and commentators.
"There is a whole cottage industry now of terrorism experts," Zogby said. "The neo-conservative commentators don't have a job if they don't have a demon."

Zogby's strategy to combat such demonisation is political. He has compiled a data base of 560,000 registered Arab voters and is trying to bring the Arab community into the mainstream political process.
"The way to end discrimination and get respect is to get a little power," he said.
He believes two more Arab Americans could win congressional seats in the November 5 election.
Arab Americans already have four seats in the House of Representatives, one in the Senate and their first cabinet place, Donna Shalala as health secretary.
Maksoud's approach is to take up civil liberties issues and, in particular, to battle the "image-makers" of Hollywood.
"Out of 168 appearances of Arabs in movies last year, 148 were negative" she says.

She says movie-makers who bend over backwards to avoid hurting the sensibilities of Jews, blacks, native Americans and other minorities still portray Arabs as terrorists, gold-diggers, villains who are cruel, craven or just plain dirty.
The ADC's biggest struggles have been with the Walt Disney Company. After lobbying, the ADC got Disney to drop a line from a song in the video version of their film "Aladdin".
"We got them to drop the part about cutting off ears, but not the rest."
The song paints the Arab world as:
"A faraway place, where the caravan camels roam,
"Where they cut off your ear if they don't like your face.
"It's barbaric, but hey, it's home."
